newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss petition attacks bankers, leaders over Jews.
newsitem.headline: Swiss petition attacks bankers, leaders over Jews.

text.p: A petition signed by Swiss professionals decried on Wednesday the stance of the country's leaders and bankers in the dispute over the fate of Jewish funds, calling it an insult to Jews.

The petition by several hundred lawyers, artists, teachers, doctors and journalists said the authorities had left Swiss Jews to confront anti-semitism on their own by failing to declare anti-semitism and racism unjustifiable.
"We, the undersigned nationals and residents of Switzerland, feel discredited by the behaviour of our country's banks and Federal Council (cabinet)," it said.
"We consider it all the more imperative that recent Swiss history be further freed of distortion and embellishment, and be rewritten with greater honesty and truth."
Jewish groups say Switzerland profited from billions of dollars of unclaimed bank accounts of victims of the Holocaust, the Nazi drive to eliminate Jews, and they want compensation.

Members of the roughly 30,000-strong Jewish community in Switzerland say anti-Jewish feeling, long suppressed in Swiss society, is now surfacing in letters and telephone calls to Jewish groups and virulent letters to newspapers.

The petition criticised Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, who dismissed Jewish calls for quick compensation as "extortion and blackmail" last month but later apologised, saying he had hurt Switzerland's credibility.
"It is an insult not only to the Jewish people but to all the democratically-minded inhabitants of our country," it said.

Many Swiss have rallied behind Delamuraz, whose comments as he finished a one-year term in the rotating Swiss presidency raised hackles abroad and triggered threats that Jewish groups might boycott Swiss banks.

The controversy was fanned this month when Union Bank of Switzerland was caught destroying historical documents days before a law banning the destruction of data that could be used in investigating Jewish assets came into force.
"If the largest Swiss bank destroyed big quantities of documents...then the Swiss authorities should no longer align their policy to the interests of these banks," the petition said.

"Swiss banks are continuing to behave, after more than fifty years, as if the role of Swiss financial marketplace as a willing helper of the Nazis and recipient of their stolen goods were not already well and widely known."
